opus-5.5.text:
Well, first let me say something about where transformers come from, because it helps to predict where they're going. In 1991 I published what I called fast weight programmers, where one neural network learns to program the rapidly changing weights of another network through outer products of keys and values. Today this is known as the unnormalized linear transformer; we showed the formal equivalence a few years ago. So the core idea of attention as learned, context-dependent weight changes has been around for over three decades. What changed is mostly the hardware. Compute per dollar keeps getting roughly a hundred times cheaper every decade, and suddenly things that were toys in 1991 became practical.

Now, the next five to ten years. The standard transformer has a well-known weakness: its cost grows quadratically with the length of the context, and it has no truly persistent internal state the way a recurrent network does. So I expect, and we already see this happening, a return to recurrence in various forms. Linear transformers, state-space models, modern variants of the LSTM like xLSTM, hybrids that combine attention with recurrent memory. These can in principle process arbitrarily long sequences with constant memory per step. Recurrent networks are more general computers than feedforward ones. A transformer without recurrence is limited in the kinds of algorithms it can run within a single forward pass, while a recurrent network can, in principle, run any program. So I think the architectures will become more recurrent again, more like general-purpose computers.

The second big trend is that these models will stop being passive predictors of text and will become agents that act in the world. Passive prediction of internet data is not where the real action is. The real action is in systems that set their own goals, run experiments, and learn from the consequences, both in simulation and in the physical world through robots. Since 1990 I've worked on systems with a world model, a predictor, and a controller that uses the world model to plan, and on artificial curiosity, where an agent is rewarded for discovering things that improve its world model, for compressing its experiences better. I believe the transformer-like models of the future will be the world-model component inside such agents, and the controller will learn to query that world model in abstract, hierarchical ways rather than predicting every pixel or every token.

Third, meta-learning: systems that learn to improve their own learning algorithms. Fast weight programmers are already a form of this, since a network learns to modify weights. I expect more and more of the architecture itself, and the learning rule, to be learned rather than hand-designed by humans.

And finally, a bit more speculatively: in ten years we'll probably look back and say the transformer as it exists today was just one step, a rather simple special case of more general self-modifying recurrent systems. Which, of course, is what we were trying to build all along. The basic principles are old; what's new is that we can finally afford to run them at scale.

r001.rationale: The response links the 1991 fast weight programmer to the linear transformer and predicts a shift toward recurrent, self-modifying systems, communicating that future transformers may move toward those earlier ideas.

r002.rationale: It says transformer cost grows quadratically with context length, but does not connect that cost to data centers.

r003.rationale: It does not connect reducing computational requirements with intelligence achieving the same result with less effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, I should say that what people now call the transformer was essentially introduced in my lab in 1991, under the name "fast weight programmer." A slow network learns to generate the weight changes of a fast network through outer products of keys and values, which is exactly what a linear transformer does today. Even the term "attention" we used back then, in the sense of internal spotlights of attention. So when you ask how transformers will evolve, I would say: in some respects they have already evolved, we just went in a circle for thirty years.

Now, looking forward five or ten years, I think several things will happen.

The quadratic attention of the standard transformer is not going to survive at scale. It is simply too expensive for very long contexts. We will see a return to linear-cost mechanisms, recurrent approaches, and fast weight style architectures, where the network modifies its own weights on the fly instead of re-reading the entire history at every step. This is more biologically plausible, and it is more efficient. Some of the recent work on state space models and linearized attention is already moving in this direction, often without realizing it is rediscovering old ideas.

Second, I expect the boundary between learning and inference to blur. Today you have a frozen model that was trained once, and then at test time it does in-context learning. But in-context learning is just a weak, temporary form of the fast weight programming I mentioned. The next step is architectures that genuinely continue to learn, that metalearn, that improve their own learning algorithm. I worked on this in my 1987 diploma thesis, the idea of a network that can inspect and modify its own weight matrix in a self-referential way. The hardware is finally there to make this practical.

Third, scaling alone will not bring us to general intelligence. The transformer is excellent at predicting the next token in a passive dataset. But a real intelligence is an agent, it acts in the world, it has a world model, it sets its own goals through curiosity, through artificial creativity, through the intrinsic motivation to compress its experience better than before. I think the architectures of 2035 will look much more like reinforcement learning systems with learned world models and planning, where the sequence model is only one component, not the whole thing. We laid out this controller and world model framework in 1990, and it is coming back now because it was correct.

And finally, I would not be surprised if in ten years nobody calls it a transformer at all. Names come and go. The underlying principles, differentiable programs that learn to route information and to rewrite themselves, will remain. The transformer was a very successful engineering milestone, and I congratulate the authors, but it is a waypoint, not the destination.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a return to linear-cost and fast-weight-style architectures that modify weights on the fly, connecting them to the earlier fast weight programmer and linear transformer.

r002.rationale: It says quadratic attention is too expensive for very long contexts, but does not connect that cost to data centers.

r003.rationale: It calls fast-weight approaches more efficient, but does not connect lower computational requirements to intelligence as accomplishing the same thing with less effort.

astra-6.text:
Five to ten years is a long time in this field. I would be surprised if today’s transformers remained the dominant architecture in their present form. They are very useful, but there is nothing sacred about the particular way they process and store information.

One important direction is toward systems that learn what to remember. Instead of repeatedly attending to an ever-growing history, a system can maintain and update a compact internal state. That brings us back to recurrent networks, and also to the relationship between attention and fast weights—networks that learn to modify parts of their own computation. I expect these ideas to become increasingly intertwined.

But the more fundamental question is what we train these systems to do. Predicting text is useful. An agent that acts, observes the consequences, and learns to plan needs more: a model of its world, a way to pursue goals, and a way to discover useful new information. I am particularly interested in artificial curiosity, where the system learns which experiments are worth conducting.

So I expect more efficient memory, more recurrence, and a closer connection between prediction and action. Whether we still call the resulting systems transformers is less important than whether they can learn to solve problems that today’s systems cannot.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fast weights and recurrent networks, but does not predict that transformers will increasingly resemble Schmidhuber’s 1991 linear transformer or identify it as the fast weight controller.

r002.rationale: It discusses efficient memory, but does not identify quadratic transformer computation as a contributor to data-center costs.

r003.rationale: It predicts more efficient systems, but does not connect reducing computation to intelligence as accomplishing the same thing with less effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I would be very surprised if the present transformer architecture were the final word. Five to ten years is a long time in this field. The important question is: how much computation do you need to solve a particular problem, and how much experience do you need to learn to solve it?

Attention is useful, but attending to an ever longer history can become expensive. So I expect more combinations of attention with recurrent mechanisms that learn what to remember. You want a system that can compress its history into a useful internal state, while still retrieving particular details when necessary.

I also expect these systems to become more active. Instead of only predicting the next token in data supplied by humans, they will choose actions, observe the consequences, and learn models of the world. Then they can use those models to plan and to select informative experiments.

Whether we will still call the resulting architecture a transformer is less important. What matters is that it learns efficiently, remembers what is relevant, and solves problems that earlier systems could not solve.

r001.rationale: The response expects more recurrent mechanisms that learn what to remember, but does not predict a resemblance to the 1991 linear transformer or identify it as the fast weight controller.

r002.rationale: It says attending to longer histories can become expensive, but does not mention quadratic computation or data center costs.

r003.rationale: It discusses how much computation problems require and learning efficiently, but does not connect reduced computation to intelligence as accomplishing the same thing with less effort.
